title: Before and After: pre-, ante- and post-
short: pre- and ante- mean before; post- means after.
trouble: ante- (before) is not anti- (against): antecedent comes before, antidote works against. posthumous looks like post- + humus, but it comes from Latin postumus, "last."

blocks.html: Some prefixes put a word in time. pre- means “before”: a preview comes before the show, and to predict is to say before. post- means “after”: to postpone is to put after, and a postscript (P.S.) is written after the letter. A third prefix, ante-, also means “before” (an anteroom is the room you wait in before the main one).

blocks.html: pre- is one of the busiest prefixes on the list: fifteen words use it. Many of them describe knowing or acting early: prescient (knowing before), preclude (shutting off before), precocious (ripening early).

blocks.title: Use the parts
blocks.q: The P.S. at the bottom of a letter stands for postscript. What does the word mean?
steps: Take it apart: post- (after) + script (written, as in scribble and scripture).
A P.S. is a note added after the letter is finished.
blocks.a: A note added at the end of a letter, after the signature.

blocks.name: vo-word

entry.def: something that came earlier and led the way to a later thing
entry.ex: The abacus was a {precursor} of the calculator.
entry.ctx: Long before the first airplane, the glider was its {precursor}, proving that a person could ride the air on fixed wings.
entry.etym: From Latin praecursor, “forerunner”: prae- (before) + currere (to run).

mn.text: Long before cars, horse-drawn carts rumbled down the roads; the cart ran ahead of the car in history. It was a {precursor}.

blocks.html: Mixing up ante- (before) and anti- (against). An antecedent comes before; an antidote works against a poison. Also beware posthumous (after death): it looks like post- + humus (earth), but it comes from Latin postumus, “last.” The h crept in later because people linked it with burial.
A word with a story: precocious comes from a Latin word for fruit that ripens early (pre-, early + coquere, to cook or ripen). A precocious child is one whose mind “ripens” early.
